claims.text: In titanium-rich, heavy-transition-metal HEAs outside established Nb-Ta systems, superconducting transition temperature is primarily governed by average valence electron count.
Average valence electron count modulates the strength of electron-phonon coupling.
Atomic disorder mediates pair-breaking in these HEAs.
Substitution between heavy elements having different valence electron counts will systematically tune Tc if the solid-solution structure is maintained.
The proposed starting material is a titanium-rich, single-phase, disordered solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 at.% each.
The proposed starting material has a body-centered-cubic structure.
The intervention can change average electron count while preserving the overall disordered bcc structure.
Random atomic arrangements and local lattice distortions influence electron-scattering rates and electron-phonon coupling.
Average valence electron count sets the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Average valence electron count sets the electron-phonon coupling constant.
Increasing electron count up to an optimum enhances electron-phonon interaction and increases Tc.
Excessive disorder or elements with localized or pair-breaking electronic states can increase scattering and suppress superconductivity.
Tc will vary non-monotonically with average electron count, increasing toward an optimum and then decreasing when pair-breaking becomes dominant.
Relative to the baseline, a slight increase in valence-electron density will raise Tc.
Compositions pushed beyond the optimum electron count will have lower Tc than the optimum composition.
Titanium-containing heavy-element HEAs have previously exhibited superconducting transition temperatures in the approximate range contemplated for the baseline.
Maintaining a single-phase disordered solid solution ensures that electron count and disorder, rather than precipitation or phase separation, govern superconducting behavior.
Subtle changes in lattice parameters may alter phonon spectra and thereby affect superconductivity.
